<reason>CON ran a genuinely inventive route: concede the harm, then argue the motion is a mere timing rule that launders the ambush into compliance and crowds out true all-in pricing. It executed that line with excellent textual discipline, repeatedly catching PRO adding words to the motion ("where comparison is still possible," "enforcers judge substance") and turning PRO's "quote the fee right after the address" concession against PRO's own sunk-cost harm story. Those were the debate's cleanest hits. But CON never escaped the structural problem PRO identified early and pressed to the end: CON's own cure — the headline number must be the number you pay — fully satisfies the proposition, since an all-in advertised price is by definition disclosed before the final checkout screen. A floor is not a ceiling. So CON's only route to a NO vote rests entirely on the speculative claim that adopting the weaker rule consumes "the one legislative moment" and hands firms a decade-long defense. That mechanism was asserted, not supported, and PRO answered it squarely: the status quo is the real safe harbor, since today the reveal happens only where resistance dies, whereas a written early disclosure is scrapeable, screenshottable, and enforceable. CON's Q2 answer ("there is no honest reason" to reveal only at payment) was admirably honest but conceded that voting no preserves a practice CON itself calls indefensible. PRO's answers were less textually tidy but comparatively decisive: address entry costs seconds, payment surrenders money, so moving the reveal upstream converts a trap into a choice. On the motion as written, PRO gave the cleaner reason to vote; CON gave the cleverer reason to wish for a better motion.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's [B2.1]-[B2.6] was the sharpest single exchange, showing PRO rewriting the motion's text and relocating rather than removing the ambush. But PRO's decisive counter across [A2.2], [A4.4] and [A5.2] neutralized its impact: CON's preferred all-in rule itself satisfies the proposition, so voting no protects the very payment-screen ambush CON admits has "no honest reason," on nothing more than an unsupported crowd-out prediction — "perfection that preserves deception is not principle, it is permission."</best_rebuttal>
